phrases: At twenty-three minutes past one in the morning, an operator at Chernobyl pressed the emergency shutdown button.
Seconds later, reactor number four exploded.
The button meant to stop the reactor helped to destroy it.
To see how, we need to look inside an R B M K reactor.
The fuel is uranium, packed into long rods.
When a uranium atom splits, it releases heat, and a few neutrons that can split more atoms.
A chain reaction.
Those neutrons work best when they're slowed down.
In an R B M K, that's done by a huge stack of graphite blocks.
Water is pumped up through more than a thousand channels in the graphite.
It boils, and the steam spins turbines that make electricity.
To control it all, rods of boron, which swallows neutrons, slide in and out from above.
Here's the catch.
The cooling water also absorbs some neutrons.
When it turns to steam, it absorbs fewer.
More neutrons, more splitting, more heat, more steam.
Engineers call it a positive void coefficient.
At low power, it made this reactor unstable.
Most reactors in the West are designed the other way round.
If their water boils away, the reaction slows down.
On the night of April the twenty-sixth, nineteen eighty-six, the crew was running a safety test, to see if a spinning-down turbine could keep the water pumps going during a blackout.
The test had been delayed by about ten hours, and handed to the night shift.
Power fell far too low, and the reactor was choked by xenon, a by-product that also swallows neutrons.
To push the power back up, the operators pulled out almost all the control rods.
Far more than the rules allowed.
Then the test began.
As the turbine slowed, the pumps slowed, less water flowed, and more of it boiled.
At one twenty-three and forty seconds, the button marked A Z five was pressed.
Every control rod began to drive in.
But the rods had a fatal design flaw.
Below the boron, each one carried a long section of graphite.
It was there to make the rods more effective, by keeping water out of the channel when a rod was pulled out.
But with the rods pulled almost all the way out, the first thing to slide into the bottom of the core was that graphite, pushing the water out.
So for the first few seconds, the shutdown button added power at the bottom of the reactor, instead of taking it away.
And the rods were slow.
Around eighteen seconds to go all the way in.
The power spiked to many times its normal level, in a few seconds.
Fuel shattered, water flashed into steam, and the pressure burst the fuel channels.
The rods jammed, partway in.
A steam explosion threw the reactor's massive steel lid, weighing at least a thousand tonnes, up through the roof.
Seconds later, a second explosion scattered burning graphite and fuel across the site.
The graphite burned for days, and the smoke carried radioactive material across Europe.
Two workers died that night.
Dozens more died from radiation in the months that followed, and the long-term toll is still debated.
Every other R B M K was changed.
The control rods were redesigned, and a faster emergency shutdown system was added.
The fuel was made slightly richer, and extra absorbers were added, to tame that feedback loop.
And the minimum number of rods that must stay in the core was raised sharply.
An international safety review later concluded that the reactor's design flaws were central to the disaster, not just the operators' mistakes.
Today, reactor four sits under a giant steel arch, slid into place in twenty sixteen.
A safety button that can make things worse isn't really a safety button.
What other machine do you know with a button that could backfire?
Tell me in the comments.
